title: Scientists may have discovered new branch on the human family tree, 100,000-year-old tooth in China suggests
summary: One tooth from a cave in southern China may upend how we think about early human origins in Asia.
content: In a cave in southern China, archaeologists have discovered an unusual 100,000-year-old tooth that may add a brand-new branch to the human family tree. A genetic analysis of the enamel revealed that the tooth is distinct from all other examples discovered in the area and may have come from an individual who belonged to a previously unknown ancient human lineage. In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Nature , researchers described four isolated teeth recovered from two cave sites in southern China that date to around 100,000 years ago, when our extinct cousins the Denisovans roamed Asia. Teeth from one cave site are similar to Denisovans', but a tooth from the second site has a unique shape and genetic variants in the tooth enamel, suggesting it is from an "unresolved archaic Homo " group, the researchers wrote. The teeth were recovered from archaeological cave sites named Longchuandong and Chuanshandong in the Guangxi region. Based on uranium-series dating , the two teeth from Longchuandong — a molar and a bicuspid (the teeth between the canines and molars) — date to about 104,500 to 42,600 years ago, while the two teeth from Chuanshandong — which are both bicuspids — are at least 100,800 years old. To try to figure out which ancient human group these teeth belonged to, the researchers studied the shape and characteristics of the teeth and extracted proteins from the tooth enamel. The heritable traits of the two Longchuandong teeth lined up well with Denisovan teeth that had previously been identified, revealing that a Denisovan-related group was living in southern China in the Late Pleistocene (129,000 to 11,700 years ago), according to the study. But the Chuanshandong teeth — which the team thinks may be from the same individual — were very different. The shape of the Chuanshandong bicuspids "did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member," the researchers wrote. For example, the Chuanshandong teeth had a complex tooth root system typically seen in Homo erectus , but they also had traits more aligned with Homo sapiens , including a more symmetrically shaped tooth crown. The root system of the Chuanshandong tooth was complex and similar to what experts see in Homo erectus . (Image credit: Qiaomei Fu / Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology) The researchers extracted proteins from the Longchuandong teeth and one of the Chuanshandong bicuspids and discovered they were all from chromosomally male individuals. But while the Longchuandong proteins matched those from Denisovan remains that were unearthed elsewhere in China, several of the Chuanshandong protein variants have only been identified in H. erectus and Homo antecessor , an ancient human distantly related to Neanderthals and modern humans. The protein analysis "showed that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens ," the researchers wrote in the study. This means that "at least two non- sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China's subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene," they wrote. A new branch? Given the small number of 100,000-year-old fossils from China that have been analyzed to date, it is unclear what the morphology and genetics of the Chuanshandong teeth mean for our understanding of human evolution , researchers say. Denisovans were first identified in 2010 , when DNA analysis of a tiny pinkie finger bone found in a Siberian cave revealed that the group was distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans. Since then, paleoanthropologists have discovered fossils all across Asia from our extinct cousins and learned that Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans all interbred when they had the chance. But Denisovans' and Neanderthals' genetics are known from full genomes — the complete set of their genetic material — while due to preservation issues, most of the fossils from China have only produced proteomes , a more limited set of genetic data that provides information on the body's proteins. The Chuanshandong proteome included an ancestral genetic variant linking them to H. erectus and H. antecessor , two groups that lived before H. sapiens arrived on the scene. The presence of these variants suggests that the Chuanshandong teeth were from someone who belonged to a primitive Homo lineage, the researchers wrote. Their unique ancient proteins could also be explained by interbreeding with H. erectus . It's not clear whether they are our cousins. Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in China It's too early, though, to call this a new human group, study co-author Qiaomei Fu , director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email. "We could call it the Chuanshandong group temporarily, but we need more fossil and molecular evidence to determine its affinity with other archaic Homo ," Fu said. "It's not clear whether they are our cousins." The Guangxi region of China is known for its caves, many of which have Pleistocene mammal fossils. (Image credit: Getty Images) "There is more to learn" The new Chuanshandong proteome is extremely interesting, said John Hawks , an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. But "the paper characterizes this as an 'unknown Homo '. I wouldn't put it that way. The question is which group has variation of the proteome," he told Live Science in an email. Hawks noted that it is currently unclear whether H. erectus or Denisovans had the specific variant identified in the Chuanshandong tooth, as paleoproteomic analysis is still a relatively new technique. If the genetic variant existed in H. erectus , then the Chuanshandong teeth, which are more similar to H. erectus in shape than they are to Neanderthals, may actually be from an H. erectus individual rather than a brand-new human group. But the comparison is further complicated by the fact that no one has yet found other Denisovan bicuspids — the type of tooth found in the Chuanshandong cave. RELATED STORIES Homo erectus and Denisovans may have lived alongside each other in China, study suggests Our extinct cousins the Denisovans had a 'distinctive' appearance, new analysis reveals Enigmatic Denisovans lived by cave in what is now China for 100,000 years, rare fossils and handcrafted tools reveal "I have a feeling that a comprehensive analysis with all the teeth together would be stronger than these separate papers " that Fu's research team has published recently, Hawks said. "I think there is more to learn from compiling more complete analyses." The researchers noted in the study that excavations have been ongoing in Guangxi caves for a decade, revealing a rich variety of Pleistocene mammal fossils, including ancient human relatives. This may mean that the pace of discoveries about our species' past will soon accelerate. "We have some new findings from this region, and we are conducting analyses on them," Fu said. title: A woman gulped ice-cold drinks and ended up with torn arteries
summary: A woman's heart issues seemed to be tied to her rapid gulping of ice-cold drinks.
content: The patient: A 46-year-old woman in California The symptoms: After an uneventful 10-hour work shift, the woman was walking to her car and drinking an ice-cold beverage when a sudden, burning pain struck the middle of her chest. The pain spread to both of her forearms and lasted about 20 minutes. About 10 minutes after this pain began, she started sweating and felt nauseated and lightheaded, as though she might pass out. What happened next: The pain continued as the woman began driving home, so she changed course and instead drove to the nearest emergency department. An electrocardiogram (EKG), which records the heart's electrical activity, showed subtle abnormalities. A blood test for troponin, a protein released into the bloodstream when heart muscle is damaged, was normal. However, a second troponin test taken before she left the hospital came back elevated after she had been discharged. Doctors called her about the new results and advised her to drive to the nearest emergency department. There, a third blood test showed that her troponin level had risen even further, and doctors diagnosed a heart attack . An angiogram — a scan that shows the structure of blood vessels — revealed a small tear in a branch of her right coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart. About 30 hours after she was discharged, the woman developed similar chest pain after taking several gulps of ice-cold green tea and subsequently jogging up a flight of stairs. The pain began when she reached the top of the stairs and was accompanied by the same lightheaded feeling she had experienced before. She called 911 and was again brought to an emergency department, and although an initial EKG showed no clear signs of a heart attack, subsequent recordings revealed heart-activity changes consistent with one. A second angiogram revealed a new tear in the left circumflex artery, a branch of the left coronary artery. The woman developed tears in both her right and left coronary arteries, which supply the heart with oxygen-rich blood. (Image credit: Explode via Shutterstock) The diagnosis: Doctors diagnosed the woman with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), a condition in which a tear develops in the wall of a coronary artery . In SCAD, blood collects within the artery wall, and this compresses the channel that blood normally flows through to reach the heart. As in the patient's case, this compression can sometimes trigger heart attacks by drastically restricting the heart's blood supply. Doctors also found fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) in a blood vessel in the woman's pelvis. FMD changes the structure of artery walls, making them too weak or too stiff, and it's known to occur in some people with SCAD . It may have made her arteries more prone to tearing, the doctors wrote in a report of the case . The treatment: During her first emergency department visit, doctors gave the woman aspirin, fluids, medicine for nausea and an antacid. Her chest pain eventually went away. At the second visit, doctors gave her the blood thinner heparin to reduce blood clotting and the beta-blocker metoprolol to slow her heart rate. She was discharged the following morning with prescriptions for cholesterol- and blood-pressure-lowering drugs. After the second episode, doctors gave her opioid painkillers and medicine for nausea to take as needed, along with aspirin and a cholesterol-lowering drug. The cholesterol-lowering drug was soon stopped because she did not have high cholesterol. Doctors eventually stopped the blood-pressure medication, too, after a follow-up heart ultrasound showed that the affected part of her heart was moving normally again. She continued taking nebivolol, a different beta-blocker that slows the heart rate and can reduce stress on the organ, for years after these two episodes. And for several months after the second episode, the woman avoided cold drinks on her own initiative. She gradually reintroduced them, taking small sips rather than gulping. Ten years later, she remained free of symptoms, the report noted. What makes this case unique: Years later, the woman learned that cold drinks had been linked to atrial fibrillation (AFib), an irregular heart rhythm. She told her healthcare team that she suspected cold drinks might have triggered SCAD in her case, too. Other dilemmas Man's 'silly experiment' at work led to a fatal 'rectal explosion' Mom experienced 'extreme unhappiness' only when she breastfed A man swallowed a bone, and‬ 15 years later, doctors found it in his appendix Separately, a 2017 case report described another woman who developed chest pain and a heart attack after drinking cold water. Doctors subsequently found that she had SCAD and FMD. However, that report did not investigate cold water as a possible trigger of the patient's symptoms. The authors of the current report proposed that rapidly swallowing a cold drink may trigger a brief rise in blood pressure, known as a pressor response. This is associated with increased activation of the body's fight-or-flight system , which can then release stress hormones. These changes may make the heart contract more forcefully and cause the coronary arteries to narrow temporarily, thereby increasing the forces acting on their walls. In someone whose arteries are susceptible to tears, that added stress could contribute to rips in the tissue and the accumulation of blood within the artery wall. However, the report authors stressed that they cannot establish that cold drinks caused the woman's dissections in this instance. They hope their findings will encourage doctors to ask patients with SCAD about potential triggers, but they said further research is needed to determine whether rapidly drinking cold beverages can really trigger the condition. title: Your risk of heart attack and stroke could be forecasted 30 years in advance, study suggests
summary: Researchers knew that cholesterol and blood pressure are important for estimating stroke risk, but a new study suggests these should be measured far earlier in life.
content: Cardiovascular disease has long been linked to risk factors like high blood pressure and cholesterol — but a new study suggests that these factors, combined with proteins in the blood, could help forecast people's risk of heart attack and stroke decades in advance. The new study, published Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal JAMA Network Open , took a broad view of the factors that spike the risk of stroke or heart attack . The researchers found that warning signs for these conditions can be seen in patients' health data up to 30 years before they happen. The researchers say their work shows that some understudied biomarkers — measurable signals in the blood — could be useful tools in anticipating later conditions. "We did know that there are some well-established risk factors that are related to heart disease, for example, blood pressure, cholesterol," said study co-author Dorien Kimenai , an epidemiologist at the University of Edinburgh. But "nobody really has looked at the patterns of these risk factors prior to when these people are getting cardiovascular events — not systematically." For the new study, the scientists tracked data patterns from a diverse group of nearly 114,000 healthy people over 34 years. Their data spanned four long-term health studies conducted in the U.S., U.K., and Norway. At the end of the study period, the researchers divided data from participants who were still healthy at that juncture from those who had experienced heart attacks or strokes and either died or survived the events. But even at the study's outset, these two groups' blood pressure and cholesterol data showed a clear divergence. "We did see that, even three decades before, already, that these patterns were different," said Kimenai. That suggests, she added, that the difference between the two groups likely began even earlier than that. The team also divided their participants by sex and age, finding that men and women experienced different trajectories in their cardiovascular disease risk over time. Women, on average, started with lower blood pressure than men in middle age, but that switched later in life. "It shows that the age effect is as important as the sex differences," Kimenai said. In short, both factors need to be taken into account. Dr. Sintip Pattanakuhar , a clinician scientist at the University of Strathclyde in Scotland who was not involved in the study, said that while these risk factors can't be modified in the way blood pressure or cholesterol can, age and sex could be incorporated into personalized screening programs for cardiovascular risk. During a stroke, the brain's blood supply is blocked or a blood vessel bleeds inside the organ. This reduces the blood and oxygen supply in certain parts of the brain, driving tissue damage and death. (Image credit: BSIP via Getty Images) The team also looked at the trajectories of biomarker proteins that circulate in the bloodstream and are linked to cardiovascular disease. These include cardiac troponin and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), which are released by damaged heart muscle tissue and used to diagnose a heart attack. They also included C-reactive protein, a liver-borne molecule that signals rising inflammation in the body. Differences in cardiac troponin and C-reactive protein were visible in people who would go on to have a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before they happened. For NT-proBNP, the differences emerged about 10 years before. That said, Kimenai cautioned that the biomarker data came from fewer participants than the full study cohort, so these results bear further confirmation. Dr. Deepak Bhatt , director of the Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital in New York, said the study's blood pressure and cholesterol data confirmed what cardiologists had long suspected about these risk factors: that these modifiable factors predict cardiovascular disease. Bhatt, who was not involved in the study, added that the biomarker data in this study built on other studies that have also shown that cardiovascular events can be predicted years before they happen. "What this adds is that it's actually predicting events decades before," he said. Related stories Men develop cardiovascular disease 7 years before women, study suggests. But why? People with more 'brown fat' have healthier cardiovascular systems. A new study in mice may explain why. 'Breakthrough' stem-cell patches stabilized woman's heart as she awaited transplant The study's clearest message was that people should get their cardiovascular risk factors checked early, Kimenai said. "When you're 40 years old, get your risk assessments and your blood pressure measured," she said. "Because these are the things you can change. If you've then been identified as having hypertension, then you can get those drugs that are very effective and safe and efficient to alter the pattern." However, while the value of checking blood pressure and cholesterol is well established, Kimenai and Bhatt agreed that the clinical value of the biomarker data was less clear at this stage. Bhatt said that he might advise a patient with high blood pressure to start medication and cut out salt, for example, but the way forward for someone with an elevated biomarker reading is less clear for now. "Ideally, more work will be done" to see whether panels of biomarkers, perhaps combined with tools that measure genetic risk , could flag patients at very high risk of having heart attacks and strokes and should be treated differently than a patient with lower risk, Bhatt suggested. "That's sort of the missing piece of the Holy Grail of prevention." This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice. title: 'Like designing a new key to open a defective lock': AI-designed protein tricks defective insulin receptors into working
summary: Scientists reported that an AI-designed protein can activate broken insulin receptors in lab mice, hinting at a potential new treatment for some forms of severe insulin resistance.
content: A protein designed with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) has successfully switched on faulty insulin receptors in lab mice even when insulin itself couldn't. The findings hint at a new way to treat certain rare, life-threatening genetic disorders that cause insulin resistance , in which the body's cells don't respond well to the blood-sugar-controlling hormone. In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Science Translational Medicine , researchers found that the AI-designed protein, called RF-409, lowered blood sugar and reduced damage to the pancreas in mice with a genetic form of severe insulin resistance. This, in turn, prevented dangerous weight loss that typically comes with the condition. When blood sugar rises, the pancreas releases insulin, a hormone that binds to proteins called insulin receptors on the surface of cells. This changes the receptors' shape, triggering a series of chemical signals that ultimately help bring blood sugar levels back down. But mutations in the gene that encodes the insulin receptor can disrupt this process. More than 150 such mutations have been linked to inherited forms of insulin resistance . In one of the most severe forms, called Donohue syndrome, children can experience dangerously high blood sugar after eating, and unusually low blood sugar between meals, as well as poor growth. Most children with the condition die before their first birthday . "Some [of these] patients produce extremely high levels of insulin, but their receptors cannot respond properly," study co-author Eunhee Choi , a cell biologist at Columbia University, told Live Science. "Simply giving more insulin may not solve the problem." That's why Choi and her colleagues explored whether they could activate the receptor in another way. In 2025, the researchers used computational tools, including AlphaFold2 , an AI program that predicts protein structures and how they fit together, to develop proteins that activate insulin receptors in a different way than insulin does . In that previous study, one of those proteins, RF-409, lowered blood sugar in both healthy mice and mice with obesity. In the new research, the team wanted to see whether RF-409 could also activate defective insulin receptors. First, they ran experiments with laboratory-grown mouse and rat cells and with healthy mice, both with working insulin receptors. This confirmed that RF-409 largely mimicked insulin's effects on cellular signaling and metabolism. In the mice, RF-409 had a nearly 60-fold longer half-life in the bloodstream than insulin, meaning the protein stays in circulation much longer before breaking down. "Both these features make [the finding] more than just an elegant trick," said Dr. Rajiv Agarwal , a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine who was not involved in the study. Unlike a protein that mimics only some of insulin's effects, RF-409 reproduces most of its normal signaling, "which matters in children who need growth as well as glucose control," he added. Insulin (orange) plugs into the insulin receptor (blue) to change its shape and trigger signals inside cells. The new protein activates the receptor in a different way. (Image credit: selvanegra via Getty Images) To test how RF-409 works with defective receptors, the researchers focused on a mutation previously identified in patients with Donohue syndrome; this genetic mutation alters a key part of the receptor's structure, preventing insulin from binding to it. Computer models suggested that RF-409 could bypass the affected region and hold the receptor in the shape needed to transmit signals inside cells. The researchers genetically engineered mice to carry this mutation. Compared with mice that retained a functioning copy of the insulin receptor gene, these mice had, on average, roughly 2.5 times higher blood sugar and 10 times higher fasting insulin levels (the amount of insulin in blood after a period without food). When injected with insulin, mice with defective receptors showed no substantial drop in blood sugar. Treatment with RF-409, however, lowered mice's blood sugar by roughly 60% within two hours. "It is like designing a new key to open a defective lock," said Kalaiarasan Ponnusamy , a computational biologist at SRM Institute of Science and Technology in India who was not involved in the study. "From a computational protein-design perspective, this is a major advance because it demonstrates that entirely new proteins can be engineered to restore receptor function without correcting the underlying genetic mutation." After 14 days of continuous treatment, five mice given RF-409 had lower blood sugar, maintained their body weight and retained more abdominal fat than five mice given a saline solution, for comparison. The treated mice also showed less pancreatic damage. "Extending this approach to other disease-causing receptor mutations is a realistic possibility, provided the receptor retains its ability to transmit signals," Ponnusamy said. Some mutations, for instance, prevent insulin receptors from reaching the cell surface or transmitting signals inside cells at all. That means the technique demonstrated in the study is unlikely to work against such mutations. Related stories 'A cure on the horizon': Are we finally close to ending type 1 diabetes? DeepMind's AI used to develop tiny 'syringe' for injecting gene therapy and tumor-killing drugs Scientists can now 'watermark' AI-generated proteins to deter bioweapon creation. But will it really work? Identifying which mutations can be treated in this way is now a priority for Choi. The team also plans to investigate how RF-409 affects different tissues in the body and whether it remains safe and effective over longer periods of treatment, she said. Although Agarwal foresees several hurdles in bringing RF-409 into clinical use; for instance, the immune system's reaction to the protein will have to be carefully studied, and in general, it's challenging to run trials with infants with rare disorders. That said, he remains hopeful that it could help patients whose diseases have no treatments to treat the underlying cause. "This is the first approach I have seen that addresses the actual defect rather than working around it," he said. title: Ancient 'supermountains' under Antarctica supercharged complex life on Earth, study claims ‪—‬ but not everyone agrees
summary: A study claims that ancient "supervolcanoes" hidden under Antarctica may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. But not everyone agrees.
content: Scientists have found the remnants of supermountains in the seabed around Antarctica . They say these ancient peaks may have provided the nutrients that led to an explosion of complex life millions of years later. However, others are more skeptical about these conclusions. About 600 million years ago, landmasses in the Southern Hemisphere collided to form the supercontinent Gondwana, which included what is now South America, Africa, Arabia, Madagascar, India, Australia and Antarctica. At that time, there was multicellular life, but it was very primitive. Previous research suggested that the continental collision created massive Himalaya-like mountains in what is now Antarctica. Now, in a new study, published online Sept. 12 in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters , scientists say they've found the sediment that accumulated in the oceans when the Gondwanan mountains eroded over millennia. "The results suggest that the assembly of Gondwana involved multiple major continental collisions, producing an extensive network of mountain belts comparable in scale to the modern Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau," Nathan Daczko , a petrologist at Macquarie University in Australia who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email. "The study highlights just how much geological history remains hidden beneath Antarctica." Ancient minerals Most of Antarctica is trapped beneath an ice sheet , so it is difficult to understand its evolutionary history. To address this, the team drilled into the seabed at 12 locations around Antarctica, extracting soil samples. They were looking for ancient crystals called detrital zircon. Zircon is a mineral that grows in rocks and is strong enough to remain chemically intact when the rock erodes. "We can date it very, very precisely, and from the geochemistry, and especially the trace elements, we can determine where the zircon came from," Ian Campbell, a geochemist at the Australian National University and a co-author of the study, told Live Science. They dated 1,712 zircon grains extracted from marine sediments and compared the abundance of zircons in Antarctica with a global zircon database, across different time scales. "We have used the zircon record to show that the mountains that formed during the amalgamation of Gondwana were the largest and most extensive in the history of the Earth, and they included some very high mountains like the Himalayas today," Campbell said. Alan Collins , an earth scientist at the University of Adelaide in Australia, said that he was surprised by the scale of the erosion from these rocks. "It beautifully supports ideas that the mountains that formed as the supercontinent Gondwana amalgamated were amongst the largest on Earth through deep time," he told Live Science in an email. The formation of Gondwama produced one-fifth of the world's zircons, and the creation of the supercontinent Pangaea around 320 million years ago produced 14%, the study found. Elias Rugen , a geochemist at the University of Southampton in the U.K. who wasn't involved in the research, was surprised by the "abundance of zircons associated with Gondwana's assembly in the Antarctica samples." "It is remarkable how much information about Antarctica's geological past can be recovered from these tiny minerals, particularly when so much of the continent remains hidden beneath ice," he said. However, he cautioned against estimating the range's height from the zircon data. "It is really difficult to infer a mountain's height from data like this," he said. An illustration of what the Pangea supercontinent would have looked like. (Image credit: Ianm35 via Getty Images) Sedimentary life source The formation and erosion of the Gondwana supermountains had consequences for the rest of the planet and the life on it, the authors said. "In order to get life, you need nutrients," Campbell said. "At that time, most of the life was in the oceans, so you need to get nutrients into the ocean." Today, the world's biggest ongoing erosion event is the Himalayas. This massive mountain range is eroding, and sending sediment down rivers and into the ocean. This deep-sea sediment deposit is called the Bengal Fan and is Earth's largest such deposit. In a similar way, Gondwana's massive mountains also "sent lots of nutrients into the ocean," Campbell said, which "significantly advanced the evolution of life" on Earth. Soon after the formation of Gondwana, the planet entered the Cambrian period. This era, which lasted from about 541 million to 485 million years ago, saw a dramatic diversification of life on Earth, known as the Cambrian explosion . The period saw the rise of creatures such as chordates (animals with a dorsal nerve, including humans) and arthropods (the ancestors of insects and crustaceans). The study's authors drew a link between Gondwana's supermountains and this rapid evolution of complex life. While the supermountains don't explain the Cambrian Explosion directly, they "provide the opportunity for it to happen," Campbell said. The paper suggests that these nutrients fed organisms that formed the base of the animal food web. Related stories The ozone layer was supposed to be healing. So why is this year's Antarctic ozone hole so big? Antarctica's first dinosaur fossil belonged to a group of the largest land animals ever Scientists discover giant, fan-shaped structure deep beneath the East Antarctic Ice Sheet However, Daczko and Rugen are skeptical. "The methods used in this study cannot directly demonstrate that this particular mountain belt was directly responsible for the rise in oxygen or the Cambrian Explosion," Rugen said. "However, the evidence for a Gondwanan supermountain belt that would inevitably have had a substantial impact on Earth's biogeochemical cycles is growing." Daczko said he would frame the link between the Gondwana's supermountains and the Cambrian explosion as "an exciting hypothesis rather than an established causal relationship." However, the study did show that there was much more to discover under the ice in Antarctica. "The most exciting aspect is the possibility that some of the largest mountain systems in Earth's history are effectively hidden beneath the East Antarctic ice sheet," Daczko said. "Antarctica potentially holds some of the most important remaining evidence for understanding the tectonic and environmental evolution of our planet." title: California braces for triple flooding threat as 'king tides' overlap with 'super' El Niño
summary: Exceptionally high tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and abnormally warm water are converging on California's coast, with authorities urging residents to limit unnecessary travel this Thanksgiving.
content: Major flooding of up to 2.7 feet (0.8 meters) is expected in parts of California today (Nov. 25) as record-breaking tides, El Niño -fueled conditions and warmer-than-average ocean water converge along the state's coast. The triple flooding threat is expected to hit the San Francisco Bay Area especially hard, with San Francisco International Airport and other low-lying areas of the city bracing for deluges , while officials warned of dangerous breaking waves measuring 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) tall along San Francisco's coast, the San Francisco Chronicle reported . Meanwhile, in Southern California, coastal communities should expect potentially record-breaking "king tides" and breaking waves up to 15 feet (4.6 m) high, the National Weather Service warned on its website . King tides are exceptionally high tides that occur every year due to seasonal factors and the alignment of Earth, the sun and the moon — but this year's "super" El Niño has amplified the risk by pushing a massive "Kelvin wave" up California's coast . Citing the forecast, several cities on California's central coast have closed beaches to shield people from hazards, including sudden waves that could wash beachgoers out to sea. Local authorities have also urged residents to limit unnecessary travel during the Thanksgiving holiday. "As Californians head into the holiday, take a few minutes to check travel conditions, sign up for local emergency alerts, and make a plan to keep your family safe," California governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement Tuesday (Nov. 24). The flooding comes as a perfect storm of adverse conditions has gathered on California's coastline. Scientists expected the king tides and the coastal flooding associated with them to emerge this time of the year. However, these powerful tides are now arriving on top of blistering sea temperatures due to accelerating climate change and the current El Niño event — the warm phase of a multiyear natural climate pattern that's in full swing and set to intensify through the end of the year . Ocean water expands as it warms, swelling tides and raising the risk of strong surf and big waves. As a result, this year's tides are predicted to be at their highest levels since January 1983, when tides also coincided with El Niño-fueled storms, AFP reported . Record-breaking “king tides,” combined with elevated surf and a large Pacific swell, are expected to bring significant coastal flooding to California during Thanksgiving week. (Image credit: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images) RELATED STORIES 'This is such a clear story': Climate change is supercharging El Niño to unprecedented strengths, study finds The super El Niño could cause torrential rainstorms. Americans may need to stock up on food to prepare, experts say. Super El Niño may push an already stressed climate ecosystem across a critical threshold, climate change researcher says In January 1983, "all hell broke loose," Reinhard Flick , a researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego, told AFP. "We had 13-foot (4-meter) waves offshore, the highest tides of the year, and hundreds of millions of dollars in damage. It hit Northern California, Southern California, everybody." Forecasts suggest this week's conditions won't be quite that bad. But there are risks to be aware of going into winter, especially as El Niño has yet to peak and more king tides are expected in December and January. "It could potentially be quite bad if we also have rainfall and high waves at the same time during any one of these big events, especially December and January, when rainfall generally increases on our coast," Flick said.

title: This winter's El Niño is a crystal ball for the future. We must use it as a test.
summary: A record El Niño is likely to temporarily push 2027 to temperatures we're only expecting in the late 2030s. It's a rare chance to learn how big El Niño can get says scientist Ioana Corfescu .
content: The supercharged El Niño building in the Pacific is likely to make 2027 the warmest year on record, about 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.7 degrees Celsius) warmer than the late 1800s . At today's rate of warming , the long-term average will not reach that level until the late 2030s. We should treat this preview as a test to understand just how big these events can get. That means writing down what we expect now and then learning from what happens, so we can act in time when the next major event hits. El Niño is a natural swing in the tropical Pacific that's part of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). During El Niño, trade winds, which normally blow from east to west along the equator, weaken. Warm water spreads east, and heat stored below the ocean surface escapes into the air. The World Meteorological Organization expects the central equatorial Pacific to average about 6.7 F (3.7 C) above normal from October to December this year, against a previous record of about 4.5 F (2.5 C) for a monthly average and 5.4 F (3.0 C) for a single week, both in late 2015. This is looking to be an extraordinary event with severe impacts. It's predicted we'll see widespread extreme weather , including wildfires, droughts and floods in Australia, Africa, Asia and South America. Crop production is expected to fall in major breadbaskets like India and Southeast Asia, disrupting food supplies and driving up prices. One forecast even suggested there could be over 450,000 heat-related deaths by February because of the additional warming from El Niño. We can use this extreme event to further develop and improve the models we use to forecast strong El Niño events, and to better understand the impacts we're likely to see. Three findings from one of my ongoing research projects shape how I think we should use this winter. First, the long-term temperature record we plan with is out of date. Studies have suggested that the Pacific changed in the late 1970s. According to a simple physical model, before 1980, an El Niño that warms the central Pacific above 5.4 F (3 C) was considered a once-in-1,500-year event. From 1980, it became about once in 60 years. This change lies mainly in the ocean, which since 1980 has held on to its extra warmth for about 1.5 years, rather than the 1.1 years it previously did. Plans built on the full historical record may underestimate the next El Niño , so we should be concentrating on models that represent the recent conditions. Second, El Niño may have a ceiling, and we still need to understand what sets it. Normally the western Pacific is much warmer than the east. That temperature difference is what keeps the trade winds blowing. El Niño grows by weakening those winds, which lets warm water spread east. But as the east warms, the difference shrinks, so El Niño uses up the very thing it feeds on. You can see this in the chart below. Over the past 76 years, every 1.8 F (1 C) of El Niño warming has shrunk the difference by about the same amount. At that rate, the difference runs out when the central Pacific is about 7 F (4 C) warmer than normal in the autumn months, when El Niño peaks, and as little as 3 F (2 C) in spring. No El Niño on record has gotten there in the season when events still grow. Two events, in 1983 and 1998, did run out of difference, but only in spring, when El Niño fades anyway, and both faded. This year's event has come closer than any other while still growing: in September it had the least difference left (just 0.6 C or 1.08 F) of any September on record. We will post our prediction before the peak. If El Niño keeps growing after the difference is gone, we are wrong. The further right a dot is, the stronger the El Niño. The lower it is, the smaller the temperature difference between the warm western and the cooler eastern Pacific. Each grey dot is one month since 1950. As El Niño grows, the dots slide down towards zero, where the difference runs out, at about 6 to 7 F (3.2 to 3.9 C) above normal in autumn and about 3 F (2 C) in spring. No El Niño has gone past that point. This year’s event (red) is the closest yet while still growing. (Image credit: NOAA ERSSTv5. Figure: Ioana Colfescu, University of St Andrews.) Third, artificial intelligence (AI) — a tool increasingly used for El Niño forecasts — is not a silver bullet either. In a 2025 study , an AI weather model trained without the strongest hurricanes could not forecast them. We see a similar limit in our El Niño tests. A model that learns only from a record that does not contain a large number of extreme events cannot always say how high El Niño can go. Models that instead build in the physics of an event, such as the east–west difference, are still our best bet for predicting strong El Niño events. The best forecasts this winter are likely to combine the two. So what should we do with this year? We need to be honest about the limits of our own models. Every forecast of this event — whether a simple physical model, an AI model or a full climate model — is being pushed beyond the range of events it was built and tested on. Where these models disagree, they are telling us where predictability runs out. Ranges of uncertainty are equally important as forecasts, and plans should be made with both in mind. Crops, rivers, power grids and human bodies respond to the heat they get, whether that heat is caused by an annual fluctuation or a long-term change in climate. Nations also need to be ready to assess these events, both before and after they occur. In June, the U.K.'s Government Office for Science brought scientists, forecasters and industry experts together. Its findings trace the risks to the U.K. through food, farming and energy, and warn that a very large El Niño "could result in unforeseen effects" on U.K. weather. Assessments like this should be standard for every government. Before the peak, forecasters, health services, utilities and food agencies should publish what they expect, and afterwards assess how the reality compared to the predictions. Finally, we should improve our models by measuring the event as closely as we can. The buoys, floats and satellites watching the Pacific are recording what may be the largest El Niño of the modern era, and that record will train and test the next generation of models. None of this works if each group acts alone. National weather services turn forecasts into warnings. People in government, industry and local services know what a failed harvest or a gas shortage costs. Scientists can test where prediction stops working, which is exactly where an event this size sits. These groups should agree before the peak what they will measure and how they will judge the forecasts, and meet again once it has passed. Exclusive to Live Science Pro Climate change will triple the number of days over 105 F in the US. The health impacts will be dire. 'The worry was that I was totally out of my league': How Francis Halzen bet his career on 'ghost particles' beneath the South Pole Critics will make two points. The first is that one El Niño year is not a 2030s climate. Its heat, droughts and floods fall in particular places, while long-term warming spreads differently, so the preview does not apply to every region. The second is that the numbers are uncertain. A simple model like ours, an AI model and a full climate model can each give a different ceiling. Both points are fair, but neither argument weakens the case. Crops, rivers, power grids and human bodies respond to the heat they get, whether that heat is caused by an annual fluctuation or a long-term change in climate. A 3 F annual rise due to El Niño affects those systems in the same way as a 3 F rise due to climate change will, only with less time to adapt. The El Niños of 1982 to 1983 and 1997 to 1998 cost the world economy an estimated $9.8 trillion in lost income between them, according to one study. As for uncertainty, the answer is to run as many simulations with as many different tools as we can, and to treat their spread as the measure of what we do not know. When models disagree, the real event is an excellent test bed to find out which one was most accurate. This winter, the Pacific will run an experiment we could never run ourselves. Either result will teach us something. If El Niño stops growing where the physics says it should, we gain a way to put an upper limit on the worst case. If it breaks through, the worst case is worse than our records show, and every plan built on those records needs revisiting. By this time next year we will know which model of El Niño came closest — and how well we coped with a year from the 2030s. title: Earliest monster black hole found at the universe's edge — pushing theories to their limits
summary: Scientists have discovered the earliest-known quasar lurking in the ancient universe — and it's growing at a slower rate than scientists believed possible.
content: A Euclid space telescope image of the newfound quasar (red dot in the center), which is further away than any known active galactic nucleus found yet. (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, Wolf et al. 2026) Astronomers have just discovered the earliest-known quasar — and it's 40 million years older than the previous record holder. The finding, which observed the object at just 630 million years after the Big Bang, could help researchers to better understand how black holes developed in the early universe. "Finding quasars at ever-increasing distances, at the edge of the observable universe, teaches us something about how the black holes in their centres grew," study co-author Julien Wolf , a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy, said in a statement . "The closer to the Big Bang we find them, the faster their black holes must have grown or the more massive they must have been at birth — or both." The object — estimated to have the mass of 360 million suns — was described in a new study published Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics . A quasar, short for "quasi-stellar radio source," is an incredibly bright core at the center of some galaxies — a region known as the active galactic nucleus (AGN). They form when supermassive black holes, which lurk at the hearts of most galaxies, start to binge on nearby matter. Once enough swirling material accumulates around these black holes, it heats up and glows intensely before falling into the object. What sets quasars apart from other AGNs is their sheer luminosity; they can be brighter than all the stars in a galaxy combined. Quasars were much more common early in the universe than they are today. They are thought to have peaked in number about 10 billion years ago. Observing them can give scientists important clues as to how galaxies evolve — and how their supermassive black holes develop. The quasar was discovered during the Euclid Wide Survey's scan of the sky — marked here in light yellow. Dark yellow patches show the target areas of Euclid's Deep Survey, which will repeatedly view smaller parts of the sky. (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA; ESA/Gaia/DPAC; ESA/Planck Collaboration) Because it takes time for light to travel, observing celestial objects that are very far away is tantamount to peering back in time . We see galaxies very near to Earth as they were only a few thousand years ago; conversely, we see galaxies very far away from us as they were billions of years ago, because their light is only now reaching our telescopes. The older the galaxy, the more red its light becomes as it stretches across the universe — a phenomenon called "redshift." Using data from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the European Space Agency's Euclid Wide Survey , the researchers behind the new study identified a quasar with a redshift of 8.13 — the first such object ever found with a redshift beyond 8. This makes it the oldest quasar yet observed, at approximately 13.1 billion years old. For reference, the universe itself is thought to be 13.8 billion years old. Related stories 'Baby quasars' spotted by James Webb telescope could transform our understanding of monster black holes The oldest, brightest black holes in the universe were born from violent gas attacks, new study suggests James Webb Space Telescope sees lonely supermassive black hole-powered quasars in the early universe The scientists named the object Dún Aonghasa , after a prehistoric cliff fort on the Atlantic-facing edge of Inis Mór, an island off the coast of Ireland. The name is meant to reflect the quasar's position at the very edge of our current observational frontier for the cosmos. According to the researchers, Dún Aonghasa also appears to be growing more slowly than astronomers previously thought possible, given its size. This suggests that its supermassive black hole may have gone through a massive growth spurt, followed by a period of much slower growth in the distant past. The discovery could put new constraints on black hole growth models, which are already being challenged by previous JWST detections of supermassive monsters that seem to have grown too big for their early place in cosmic history. Future observations from Euclid and JWST could help researchers test this hypothesis and see if it holds for other ancient quasars, the researchers said.
